Mr. Adams read aloud — political satire, Horace Mann, the "Epistles" of "Hosea Biglow"; Longfellow and Tennyson as their poems appeared — but the children took possession of Dickens and Thackeray for themselves. The boy Henry became a desultory reader of his father's eighteenth-century library, drifting into the mental indolence of history. Pope and Gray called for no mental effort; he was thirty before his education reached Wordsworth.

This is the story of an education, and the persons in it figure only as educators or educated. His father left his mind free play and taught him some French. Otherwise the family was an atmosphere rather than an influence. The overpowering set of brothers and sisters were replicas of one type, conscious only that they would like to control power in some form — the same could be said of an ant or an elephant. They amounted to one individual with half-a-dozen facets. Whether that type was fit to deal with life, no one knew.

Such turbulent children, given free rein, should have come to grief. No one was strong enough to control them, least of all their mother, the queen-bee of the hive, on whom nine-tenths of the burden fell. Father and mother were about equally helpless. Almost every large family produced one black sheep; that this generation of Adamses escaped surprised them as much as their neighbors. Henry Adams, a brand escaped from the burning, always looked back with astonishment at their luck. They were born, like birds, with a certain innate balance.

If school helped, it was only by reaction. The passionate hatred of school methods was almost a method in itself. He hated being herded with other boys and compelled to learn by memory things that did not amuse him. His memory was slow; he thought his mind a good enough machine if given time, but it acted wrong if hurried. Schoolmasters never gave time.

He reckoned his school-days, from ten to sixteen, as time thrown away. Between 1850 and 1900 nearly every one's existence was exceptional. For the life imposed on him he needed the facile use of only four tools: Mathematics, French, German, and Spanish. Latin and Greek he could have learned in six weeks instead of six years. He never controlled any of them.

Boy associations at fifteen were worse than none. The bar-room and billiard-room were more familiar than parents knew. Sport as a pursuit was unknown. Of all pleasures, winter sleighing was still the gayest. Books remained, as in the eighteenth century, the source of life — Thackeray, Dickens, Bulwer, Tennyson, Macaulay, Carlyle were devoured; but the happiest hours of the boy's education were passed in summer, lying on a musty heap of Congressional Documents in the old farmhouse at Quincy, reading "Quentin Durward," "Ivanhoe," and "The Talisman," and raiding the garden at intervals for peaches and pears. On the whole he learned most then.
